title: How can I make homework effective?
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Jo Castelino reflects on her history of ineffective homework, from unmarked booklets to takeaway menus, and designs a more deliberate programme for GCSE science. Homework is meant to consolidate and extend classroom learning through retrieval, interleaving and, over time, application questions that tie concepts together. She sequences the programme carefully, beginning with retrieval only until students have schemas, modelling the longer tasks in lessons, and then phasing them in. Assessment is handled through self-marking for retrieval and whole-class feedback slides for the longer task. The piece is a plan rather than a report, with a promise to revisit once implemented.
points: Homework should consolidate and extend classroom learning through retrieval, interleaving and application rather than novelty tasks.
Application questions linking earlier content to the current unit encourage transfer and help students see the curriculum as cohesive.
Longer tasks should be introduced only after students have schemas and have seen the task modelled in class.
Assessment stays manageable via self-marking for retrieval and a slide of common errors for whole-class feedback.
quotes: I have always been a bit rubbish with setting and assessing homework. There have been times when I have set ambitious long answer-style question booklets but then couldn’t bring myself to mark any of it and I didn’t have the time in lessons to go through them so students could self assess either.

For me, homework must be about consolidating and extending the learning process that happens in the classroom. I want my students to remember key facts and be able to apply these successfully to different contexts. For this to happen, I need a programme of homework in which my students review content learnt in class and retrieve information from previously learnt content.
By providing more application questions, we could encourage our students to think about concepts not as discrete units of study but as a cohesive curriculum that links together seamlessly.

The application question would be based on content learnt previously but that is linked to what we are learning currently. For example, by the time we teach Cells at KS4, students have already covered Ecology fully and would have some knowledge of adaptations, the carbon cycle, food chains and decomposition. There are clear connections between the ideas in Ecology and Cells that could be explored in an application question. To help with this, I would provide a few questions to guide students but also encourage them to make links beyond these hints.

At the start of the GCSE course, I plan to only provide practice and retrieval questions. There are two reasons for this. One, I want to ease my students into good home learning habits and two, their schemas would not be robust (or may not even exist!) in order to attempt an open-ended or comprehension application question.

As the lessons go on, I plan to trial a similar longer-style task in lesson so I can explicitly model what I expect students to do. This is incredibly important as I want my students to be well prepared when asked to complete a similar task independently.

For the second task, I would collect the homework in, read through them and make notes of common errors or misconceptions on a Powerpoint slide. I will then present this slide in the following lesson so students can annotate their own answers. Usually, when I do whole-class feedback, I write my comments on paper but by having these comments on a slide, I can look through previous slides and spot any recurring errors or misconceptions.
